meta.blurb: Dinner is cold and the host is late. Then he limps in, pale and bruised, and says he has just come back from the year 802,701. What he saw there is still waiting, deep underground.
meta.bible: Time Traveller: an inventor and scientist from Victorian England, curious, brave and never named. Narrator: a guest at the dinners who writes the story down. Filby: a lively, argumentative guest. Psychologist: a guest who doubts the idea. Medical Man: a guest. Mayor: a Provincial Mayor, a guest. Richmond: the town near London where the Time Traveller lives. London: the city. Time Machine: a small machine of ivory, brass and crystal with two Levers. Fourth Dimension: Time, in the Time Traveller's talk. Year 802,701: the year in which the Time Traveller lands. Sphinx: a white stone statue on a bronze Pedestal, with secret doors. Eloi: small, gentle, beautiful, childlike people who live above ground in the sun, and eat only fruit. Morlocks: pale, apelike people with big eyes who live underground in the dark and work machines. Weena: a small Eloi woman whom the Time Traveller saves from a river. Wells: deep shafts down into the underworld. Palace of Green Porcelain: a ruined museum made of green china. Matches and Camphor: the things he takes from the Palace. Iron bar: his weapon. Thames: the river near the Eloi. Hill: the green hill where he sleeps. Crabs: huge sea creatures on the shore of the far future. Last beach: the end of the world, a red sun, ice and darkness. Voice and tone: serious and curious, told by a man at a dinner table; dangers are real but never gory; the ending leaves the reader thinking, with one small thread of hope: two white flowers. Added for the full-length book. Thursday dinners: the weekly meals at the Time Traveller's house in Richmond, where the story is first told and finally ends. Guests: Filby, the Psychologist, the Medical Man (also called the Doctor), the Provincial Mayor, an Editor, a Journalist and a Very Young Man. Mrs Watchett: the Time Traveller's housekeeper, who crosses the laboratory in a flash as he leaves. Laboratory: the low workshop behind the house where the machine stands. Model: the small machine of brass, ivory and crystal that vanishes at the first dinner. Levers: the two levers of the machine, which the Time Traveller unscrews on the hill and keeps in his pocket until he fixes them in the sphinx. Hail: the storm in which he lands. Rhododendron: a bush on the hill. Great Hall: the huge ruined stone hall where the Eloi eat fruit and sleep together. Eloi: they eat only fruit, tire quickly, and fear the dark; there are no animals and no farms. Morlocks: they come up at night from the wells; the Time Traveller guesses they take the Eloi for food. Well-towers: the round shafts and tall chimneys with metal rungs that lead down to the Underworld. Weena: she is saved from drowning in the Thames, teaches him words, and is lost in the forest fire. Weena's flowers: the two white flowers he keeps; the narrator keeps them at the end. Palace: the Palace of Green Porcelain, a ruined museum with a huge skeleton, books that crumble to flakes, rusted machines and weapons. Camphor: a white lump he finds there that burns brightly. Matches: found in a sealed tin in the Palace. Iron bar: his weapon, broken from a rusted machine. Forest: the dark wood he must cross at night; he lights a fire and it spreads. Sphinx doors: the bronze panels in the pedestal that open as a trap; he fixes the levers and escapes. Crabs: the huge crab-like creatures on the red shore of the far future. Last beach: the shore at the end of the world, with ice, snow, a dull red sun, an eclipse and a round dark creature the size of a football. Return: the laboratory clock shows only a few hours have passed. Epilogue: the Time Traveller leaves again with a camera and never returns; three years pass; the narrator keeps the withered flowers. Voice and tone: serious and curious, told by a man at a dinner table; dangers are real but never gory; the ending leaves the reader thinking, with one small thread of hope: two white flowers.
chapters: Ghosts at the Edge of Dark
A Red Sun and Giant Crabs

beats.scene: Guests gather around a warm firelit table in a Richmond dining room
beats.summary: On Thursday evenings a group of friends dine at the Time Traveller's house in Richmond.

beats.scene: The Time Traveller stands before the fire with bright eyes, talking
beats.summary: After dinner he asks his guests to be patient with a strange idea.

beats.scene: He draws a flat line and a square in the air with one finger
beats.summary: He reminds them that a line or a flat surface on paper has no thickness and is only an idea.

beats.scene: A solid glass cube stands on the table in the lamplight
beats.summary: A real cube has length, breadth and thickness, so space has three dimensions.

beats.scene: Filby leans forward, frowning, to put a question to the host
beats.summary: Filby asks if there could be a fourth dimension, and the host says there is: Time.

beats.scene: Portraits of one man as a boy, youth and elder hang on a wall
beats.summary: He explains that portraits of one man at different ages are slices of one long life in four dimensions.

beats.scene: The Psychologist raises one finger while the others listen
beats.summary: The Psychologist objects that we move freely in space but cannot move in time.

beats.scene: A balloon rises over a green field while a crowd looks up
beats.summary: The host answers that memory takes us back, and balloons once seemed impossible too.

beats.scene: The Medical Man laughs and the Very Young Man looks puzzled
beats.summary: The guests laugh, and Filby demands proof, but the host says he is not joking.

beats.scene: The host leaves the room while his guests whisper and look at one another
beats.summary: He says he will bring something to prove it, and he goes out.

beats.scene: The host returns carrying a small glittering model of ivory, brass and crystal
beats.summary: He comes back with a small, delicate model of a machine, no bigger than a clock.

beats.scene: The Psychologist turns the little model over in his hands
beats.summary: The guests pass the model around, and the host says it is a machine for travelling through time.

beats.scene: A finger rests on a small lever beside the model on the table
beats.summary: He explains that one lever sends the machine into the future and the other sends it back.

beats.scene: The model blurs and trembles, then the table stands bare under the lamp
beats.summary: He presses the lever, and the model shivers, fades like a ghost and is gone.

beats.scene: The Psychologist stoops to look under the table while the others stare
beats.summary: The guests stare at the empty table, and the Psychologist looks underneath it in vain.

beats.scene: The host stands smiling beside the empty table with his hands open
beats.summary: He says the model has gone into time, and it is still here but moving too fast to be seen.

beats.scene: A long, low laboratory with lamps lit and a large machine under them
beats.summary: He leads the guests to his laboratory, where the full-sized machine stands half finished.

beats.scene: The narrator touches a rod of clear quartz beside a brass frame
beats.summary: The narrator inspects the machine, with its nickel, ivory and rods of clear crystal.

beats.scene: The host holds a pencil over drawings on a crowded workbench
beats.summary: He promises it will be ready by next week, and he means to explore time himself.

beats.scene: Guests in coats and hats leave through a dark hall into the night
beats.summary: The guests go home, and none of them quite knows what to believe.

beats.scene: A narrator in a coat walks up a lamplit path to a Richmond house
beats.summary: The next Thursday the narrator goes to the house again, and finds that the host is not there.

beats.scene: A note lies on the mantelpiece beside a clock that shows half past seven
beats.summary: The Medical Man reads out a note: the host is delayed, and the guests should begin dinner without him.

beats.scene: Guests sit down at a long table with one empty chair at the head
beats.summary: The guests start the meal and talk about the vanishing model.

beats.scene: An Editor and a Journalist smile at each other across the soup
beats.summary: The Editor and the Journalist laugh at the story, and the narrator tries to explain it.

beats.scene: The dining room door opens quietly while the narrator looks up
beats.summary: While the Medical Man is joking, the door opens, and the narrator, who faces it, sees the host first.

beats.scene: A pale, dusty man in torn clothes limps in with a bloody sock
beats.summary: The Time Traveller is dirty, pale, grey-haired and limping, with a cut on his chin.

beats.scene: He holds a glass of wine in a shaking hand and drinks it down
beats.summary: He asks for wine, drinks it quickly and recovers a little.

beats.scene: The guests sit in silence around the table while footsteps climb the stairs
beats.summary: He goes upstairs to wash, asking them to save him some meat, and the guests whisper about him.

beats.scene: The Time Traveller sits at the table in a clean coat, eating hungrily
beats.summary: He returns, changed, eats hungrily and says nothing until he has finished.

beats.scene: The guests gather around the fire while the host settles in his armchair
beats.summary: He promises to tell them everything if they will not interrupt, and they agree.

beats.scene: A man in a laboratory tightens one last screw on a gleaming machine
beats.summary: The Time Traveller says that he finished the machine that day, then checked every screw and sat in the saddle.

beats.scene: His hand grips the starting lever while the laboratory grows hazy
beats.summary: He pushes the lever, the laboratory goes dim, and the housekeeper walks through the room like a rabbit.

beats.scene: Day and night flicker like a black wing around a man in a saddle
beats.summary: He pulls the lever to its end, and night follows day faster and faster.

beats.scene: The traveller clings to the saddle with a white face
beats.summary: The feeling is like a headlong fall, and he dreads that the machine will crash.

beats.scene: The sun hops across the sky above a fading workshop
beats.summary: The laboratory fades away, and the sun leaps across the sky once every minute while the moon waxes and wanes.

beats.scene: A grey blur where trees grow and fade like smoke and towers rise
beats.summary: The days blur into grey, the sun becomes a streak of fire, and buildings rise and vanish like dreams.

beats.scene: Small brass dials spin while snow and spring green flash past
beats.summary: The dials race round, and he sees that he is travelling a year every minute.

beats.scene: A hand hovers over the lever, trembling
beats.summary: He fears that the machine may stop where something solid stands, and he decides to slow down.

beats.scene: He drags the lever back and the blur begins to slow
beats.summary: The world slows, ghostly shapes become solid, and the machine comes towards the end of its journey.

beats.scene: The machine tips over on a hillside and the traveller flies through the air
beats.summary: The machine tips over suddenly and throws him through the air.

beats.scene: A wet man rises from grass while hail rattles around him
beats.summary: He stands up, bruised and soaked, in a storm of hail, with the machine lying on its side.

beats.scene: A dripping rhododendron bush stands on a grey hillside in the hail
beats.summary: He looks around at a grey hillside and a bush, and sees that the world has changed.

beats.scene: A giant white stone sphinx with raised wings stands on a bronze base
beats.summary: Through the storm he sees a huge white sphinx on a bronze pedestal, with a face worn by the weather.

beats.scene: The traveller stares up at the stone face as the storm passes
beats.summary: He feels a rush of fear, and wonders what sort of people live in this world.

beats.scene: The traveller pulls the machine upright and takes two levers from it
beats.summary: As the sky clears, he stands the machine up and puts the two levers in his pocket to keep it safe.

beats.scene: A slight figure in a purple tunic runs through the thinning rain
beats.summary: A small, beautiful person in a purple tunic comes running along a path towards him.

beats.scene: Little people in soft bright robes gather around the traveller
beats.summary: More of the small people arrive, and gather in a circle around him.

beats.scene: A small hand touches the traveller's sleeve while the others watch
beats.summary: They touch him gently and speak in soft, sweet voices that he cannot understand.

beats.scene: The traveller points at the sky and the little people laugh
beats.summary: He points at the sky and makes a noise like thunder, and the little people only laugh.

beats.scene: Flowers fall around the traveller's neck as the people sing
beats.summary: They hang flowers around his neck, and lead him down the hill.

beats.scene: A green valley with huge strange buildings and flowering bushes
beats.summary: At the foot of the hill he sees a lovely valley with huge buildings, but no fences, hedges or farms.

beats.scene: The traveller stops suddenly and looks back at the hilltop
beats.summary: He remembers the machine and runs back up the hill, with the little people following him.

beats.scene: A flattened patch of grass beside the sphinx's bronze base
beats.summary: The machine is gone, and only a flat patch of grass and some deep marks remain.

beats.scene: Furrows in the wet grass lead to the bronze pedestal
beats.summary: The marks lead him to the pedestal, and he searches wildly round the statue and the bushes.

beats.scene: The traveller beats on the bronze panels of the pedestal
beats.summary: He raps on the bronze panels and hears that they sound hollow, as if something is inside.

beats.scene: The little people look away awkwardly while he knocks
beats.summary: The little people seem uneasy about his knocking, and they politely turn away from him.

beats.scene: The traveller sits on the grass with his head in his hands
beats.summary: He understands that he is stranded in the future, but he finds hope in the levers in his pocket.

beats.scene: Evening light falls on a huge stone doorway, carved and weathered
beats.summary: As evening comes, the little people lead him to a great ruined hall with a huge carved doorway.

beats.scene: A circle of little people sit on cushions around the traveller
beats.summary: Inside the hall they sit around him, and he tries to ask about the machine, but they do not understand.

beats.scene: The traveller points at objects while the little people say their names
beats.summary: He begins to learn their language by pointing at things and listening to the names.

beats.scene: A stone table piled with strange fruit in a great hall
beats.summary: The little people bring him strange fruit, and he finds that they eat nothing else.

beats.scene: A vast hall with cushions on the floor and no kitchens or doors
beats.summary: He sees that the great buildings have huge halls but no kitchens, no fires and no private rooms.

beats.scene: Dozens of little people sleep in rows on cushions under pale moonlight
beats.summary: At night all the little people sleep together in the halls, and nobody sleeps alone.

beats.scene: An empty green valley with no horses, cows or dogs
beats.summary: He sees no cows, horses or dogs, and no one at work in the fields.

beats.scene: Small figures in matching soft clothes laugh in a field of flowers
beats.summary: The men and women look nearly alike in size and dress, and they behave like children.

beats.scene: The traveller sits on the hillside while the sun sets over the valley
beats.summary: He sees no one old or ill, and wonders where the elders of this people have gone.

beats.scene: A crumbling granite ruin with fallen tiles and a broken wall
beats.summary: He walks among huge ruins and sees that the old world has fallen to pieces.

beats.scene: Little people fall asleep in the sun in the middle of a game
beats.summary: He sees that they tire in a moment, and cannot hold their attention for long.

beats.scene: The traveller sits thinking with his chin on his hand in the sun
beats.summary: He believes they are the result of a world that has no danger and no need to struggle.

beats.scene: The traveller looks at the red sky over the peaceful valley at sunset
beats.summary: He writes his first theory, the sunset of mankind, and does not yet know how wrong it is.

beats.scene: A bright river runs through a green valley where the traveller walks to bathe
beats.summary: Some days later he goes down to the Thames to bathe, with several little people lounging on the bank.

beats.scene: A small figure is swept along the river while others sit and watch
beats.summary: One small woman slips into the deep water and is swept away, but nobody tries to help her.

beats.scene: The traveller dives into the river with his coat on the bank
beats.summary: He dives in, catches her and pulls her to the shore.

beats.scene: The traveller rubs the hands of a pale small woman on the grassy bank
beats.summary: He brings her round, and he is shocked that the others watch without any alarm.

beats.scene: A small woman puts white flowers in the traveller's pockets
beats.summary: When she wakes, she smiles, kisses his hand and fills his pockets with flowers. Her name is Weena.

beats.scene: Weena walks beside the traveller and points at things, saying their names
beats.summary: Weena stays with him all day, and teaches him many words of her language.

beats.scene: A small hand rests in a large one as they walk through the flowers
beats.summary: She grows fond of him and follows him everywhere, like a child.

beats.scene: Weena sits beside the traveller as he draws pictures in the dust
beats.summary: He tries to ask about his machine by drawing it, but she looks afraid and says nothing.

beats.scene: The traveller walks to the sphinx each morning and sees the closed bronze doors
beats.summary: He visits the sphinx each day, but he finds no sign of his machine.

beats.scene: Weena runs back toward the great hall as the sun sinks
beats.summary: Each evening Weena hurries home before dark, and he wonders what she fears.

beats.scene: Moonlight falls on a dark hall while Weena holds a hand tightly
beats.summary: Weena begs him to sleep inside every night, and she shakes when the dark comes.

beats.scene: A pale shape slips across a dark lawn at dusk
beats.summary: One evening he sees a pale, ghostly figure running across the grass, and it vanishes.

beats.scene: Little people huddle together in a great hall on a moonless night
beats.summary: On the darkest nights the little people crowd together in the halls, and he sees how much they fear the dark.

beats.scene: Two shining eyes gleam among the shadows of a ruin
beats.summary: He thinks he sees eyes shining in the ruins, and he wonders if his nerves are playing tricks.

beats.scene: A round well with a low stone rim and a dark mouth
beats.summary: He finds round wells with low stone rims, and he hears a thudding noise coming from them.

beats.scene: A white flower falls slowly into the dark mouth of a well
beats.summary: He drops a flower down a well and sees it pulled down into the dark by a rising current of warm air.

beats.scene: A line of tall shafts stands across the green valley
beats.summary: He sees that there are many shafts and towers across the valley, and he guesses they bring air to places below.

beats.scene: A man lies with his ear against the stone rim of a well
beats.summary: He lies at the edge and listens, and hears a steady beat, like the pulse of great machines.

beats.scene: Weena turns her face away from the well, pale and silent
beats.summary: Weena is terrified of the wells, and she will not look at them or talk about them.

beats.scene: The traveller sits on a hillside, looking at the wells in the evening
beats.summary: He wonders whether another kind of creature lives beneath the ground and keeps the world above running.

beats.scene: A man stands at dawn beside a well with a small box of matches
beats.summary: He decides to explore a well himself, takes his matches and tells Weena he will return.

beats.scene: Metal rungs lead down a stone shaft into the dark
beats.summary: He climbs over the rim and finds metal rungs set into the wall of the shaft.

beats.scene: A small circle of daylight shrinks above a climbing man in a shaft
beats.summary: He climbs down and down, his arms ache, and the noise below grows louder.

beats.scene: A dark tunnel with a faint grey light at the bottom of a shaft
beats.summary: At the bottom he finds himself in a dark, warm tunnel, where the thudding is very loud.

beats.scene: Pale shapes with big round eyes gleam in the darkness of a tunnel
beats.summary: Pale shapes move in the dark around him, and he feels something close by.

beats.scene: A match flares and lights white faces with huge eyes
beats.summary: He strikes a match and sees pale, ape-like creatures with huge eyes, who run from the light.

beats.scene: A cold, soft hand touches a sleeve in the dark
beats.summary: The match goes out, and cold, soft hands touch him in the dark.

beats.scene: The traveller swings his fist at pale arms and begins to climb
beats.summary: He lashes out, finds the rungs and starts to climb in a panic.

beats.scene: Pale hands grab at the traveller's ankles in the dark shaft
beats.summary: A hand grabs his ankle as he climbs, and he kicks himself free.

beats.scene: The traveller lies gasping on the grass beside a well in the sun
beats.summary: He climbs out of the well, with his last match gone, and lies in the sunlight, shaking.

beats.scene: The traveller sits shaking in the sun while Weena kneels beside him
beats.summary: Back in the sunlight, he knows that the pale ghosts were real, and Weena calls them Morlocks.

beats.scene: A drawing in the dust shows a line with people above and below it
beats.summary: He draws two groups in the dust and begins to see how the two kinds of people grew apart.

beats.scene: A cutaway shows rich people in sunlight above and workers in the dark below
beats.summary: He thinks that rich and poor slowly became two races, one in the sun and one in the dark.

beats.scene: Machines glow in a dark tunnel while little people sleep in sunlight above
beats.summary: He guesses that the Morlocks still work the machines and make the clothes of the little people.

beats.scene: Pale figures slip out of wells at night while the little people sleep
beats.summary: He realises that the Morlocks come up into the world at night, when the moon is dark.

beats.scene: The traveller keeps watch over sleeping Weena with a frightened face
beats.summary: He understands, with horror, that the little people are the Morlocks' food, like cattle.

beats.scene: The traveller looks from the hilltop toward the white sphinx in the distance
beats.summary: He sees that his machine must have been dragged into the sphinx and down to the underworld.

beats.scene: The traveller tries to push open the closed bronze doors of the sphinx
beats.summary: He pushes at the doors again, but they stay shut, and nobody inside answers.

beats.scene: A huge green building gleams far across the valley in the evening light
beats.summary: He remembers a huge green building he saw from the hills, and he thinks it may hold weapons.

beats.scene: Weena packs fruit into a basket beside the traveller as he plans
beats.summary: He decides to go there, and Weena insists on coming with him.

beats.scene: Weena and the traveller walk hand in hand across a sunny valley at dawn
beats.summary: They set out early on the long walk to the green building, and no other little person comes with them.

beats.scene: A broken stone bridge arches over a bright river
beats.summary: They cross the river by the ruins of an old bridge, and he thinks of how many people once passed this way.

beats.scene: Weena skips ahead through flowers while cloud shadows run over the grass
beats.summary: In the warm sun Weena laughs and runs among the flowers, chasing butterflies.

beats.scene: Weena walks in a wide circle around a well in the grass
beats.summary: They pass several wells, and each time Weena keeps far away from them.

beats.scene: The traveller lifts Weena onto his shoulders beside a stream
beats.summary: Weena tires, and he carries her on his shoulders across the stream.

beats.scene: The pair eat fruit in the shade while the sun stands high
beats.summary: They rest in the shade at noon, and he watches the sun and counts the hours of light.

beats.scene: The traveller climbs a hill and looks across a wide green plain
beats.summary: From a hill, he sees the huge green building clearly, standing like a ruined palace.

beats.scene: A great glittering ruin grows larger as the pair walk towards it
beats.summary: They walk on towards it as it grows bigger, with the sun beginning to sink.

beats.scene: A huge broken wall of green tiles with a gaping dark entrance
beats.summary: They reach its great broken wall of green tiles, with a dark doorway standing wide open.

beats.scene: The traveller looks anxiously at the low sun over the green ruin
beats.summary: He sees how low the sun is, and he knows that they have little time before dark.

beats.scene: A vast dim gallery with dusty windows and fallen green tiles
beats.summary: Inside the green palace they find a huge gallery, silent and thick with dust.

beats.scene: A giant skeleton of a long-dead beast rises in a dusty hall
beats.summary: In the hall stands the skeleton of a huge animal, and Weena clings to his hand.

beats.scene: Cracked glass cases hold fossils and stones, with labels turned to powder
beats.summary: They walk past broken cases of stones and fossils, and he sees that this was a great museum.

beats.scene: Shelves of books crumble to brown flakes in a quiet library
beats.summary: In a long gallery he finds shelves of books that have rotted into brown flakes.

beats.scene: Rusted machines stand silent in rows under a high dusty roof
beats.summary: He passes a gallery of rusting machines, which are of no use to him.

beats.scene: Rotten cases hold swords and guns eaten away by rust
beats.summary: He searches a gallery of weapons, but everything has rusted to nothing.

beats.scene: A sealed jar of white camphor sits on a dusty shelf
beats.summary: In a gallery of chemicals he finds a sealed jar of camphor, which he knows burns well.

beats.scene: A match flares in a dark gallery beside an open metal tin
beats.summary: He finds a tin of matches, and when he tries one, it lights.

beats.scene: The traveller wrenches an iron bar from a rusted machine
beats.summary: He breaks an iron bar from a rusted machine and finally has a weapon.

beats.scene: Dusk glows red through a broken window as Weena tugs at his hand
beats.summary: Through a broken window he sees the red sky, and he knows that they must leave now.

beats.scene: Weena and the traveller hurry across a dim plain with the green palace behind
beats.summary: They leave the palace at dusk, and the traveller hurries across the plain with Weena in his arms.

beats.scene: A black wall of forest rises against a deep blue evening sky
beats.summary: They reach a thick forest that lies across their way home, and the first stars come out.

beats.scene: A man carries a girl into dark trees, an iron bar in hand
beats.summary: He decides to cross the forest rather than go around, and he carries Weena in under the trees.

beats.scene: Pale shapes flit between black trunks in the dark
beats.summary: He hears soft footsteps and whispers all round him, and he glimpses white shapes among the trees.

beats.scene: A pale arm reaches from the shadows toward the traveller's shoulder
beats.summary: A hand touches his shoulder, and he swings the iron bar, and the creature falls back with a cry.

beats.scene: Weena droops, tired, in the traveller's tired arms among the trees
beats.summary: Weena is too tired to walk, and he too is exhausted, and the whispering draws closer.

beats.scene: A small ring of dry sticks and leaves lies in a forest clearing
beats.summary: He decides to make a fire, and gathers dry twigs and leaves in a small clearing.

beats.scene: A match flares among dry twigs and the flames leap up
beats.summary: He lights the twigs with a match, and the flames leap up and drive the whispers back.

beats.scene: Pale shapes with huge eyes circle beyond the firelight
beats.summary: In the light of the fire he sees many pale creatures, circling at the edge of the dark.

beats.scene: Flames spread up through dry trees while the traveller guards Weena
beats.summary: The fire catches the dry bushes and trees, and it begins to spread faster than he expected.

beats.scene: Red flames roar through the trees while a man lifts a sleeping girl
beats.summary: He wakes Weena and lifts her, and the heat and the roar of the fire drive them away from the clearing.

beats.scene: Burning branches fall in showers of sparks through dark smoke
beats.summary: Burning branches crash down around them, and sparks fill the air.

beats.scene: The traveller swings an iron bar at pale shapes in the red smoke
beats.summary: The Morlocks, dazzled and afraid, stumble blindly through the smoke, and he fights them with the bar.

beats.scene: Thick smoke fills the forest while the traveller coughs and stumbles
beats.summary: The smoke grows so thick that he coughs, and he loses his way among the burning trees.

beats.scene: The traveller stares at his empty arms in the red smoke
beats.summary: He suddenly realises that Weena is no longer with him.

beats.scene: The traveller shouts into the roaring smoke, searching
beats.summary: He calls her name and searches through the smoke, but no answer comes.

beats.scene: The traveller staggers out of a burning wood onto an open hill
beats.summary: The fire drives him out of the forest, and he cannot find her, and he cannot go back.

beats.scene: A man lies on a grey hillside as dawn spreads
beats.summary: At dawn he lies exhausted on an open hillside, with the forest still burning below.

beats.scene: A black wood smokes in the grey morning light
beats.summary: He searches the burnt wood in the dawn light, but he finds only ashes and silence.

beats.scene: The traveller sits alone in the ashes with his head bowed
beats.summary: He sits alone in the ashes, and he knows that he will never see Weena again.

beats.scene: A man wakes on a grey hillside under the high morning sun
beats.summary: He wakes late, and he knows that his only hope is to go back to the sphinx.

beats.scene: The traveller walks past the great hall where little people play in the sun
beats.summary: He walks back through the valley, where the little people play and eat as if nothing has happened.

beats.scene: The white sphinx rises on a green hill above a bronze pedestal
beats.summary: He climbs the hill toward the white sphinx and wonders how he can open its doors.

beats.scene: The bronze panels of the pedestal stand open, showing a dark space

A1A2: Every Thursday, some friends ate dinner at the Time Traveller's house in Richmond.
After dinner, he stood by the fire and asked his friends to listen.
He said that a line on paper has length, but no thickness.
He said that a real box has length, width and height.
Filby asked about a fourth dimension, and the host said that it is Time.
He said that pictures of a man at different ages show one long life.
The Psychologist said, “We can walk in space, but not in time.”
He said men fly in balloons now, so they may travel in time.
Filby laughed and said, “It sounds like nonsense, so please show us some proof.”
The Time Traveller said, “Wait here,” and he left the room, smiling.
He came back with a small machine made of brass, ivory and crystal.
The friends held it in their hands and looked at it carefully.
He said, “This lever goes forward in time, and this one goes back.”
He pressed the lever, and the little machine shook and then was gone.
Everyone stared at the empty table, and the Psychologist looked under it.
The Time Traveller said it was still there, but moving too fast to see.
He took his friends to his workshop, where a much bigger machine stood.
The narrator looked at the bars of crystal and the shining brass.
The host said it would be ready next week, and he would use it.
The friends went home, and nobody knew what to believe.
The next Thursday, the narrator went to the house, but the host was away.
The Medical Man read a note, and it said, “Please begin dinner without me.”
So the guests sat down to eat, and they talked about the little machine.
The Editor and the Journalist laughed, and the narrator tried to explain.
Suddenly the door opened, and the narrator saw the Time Traveller first.
He was dirty, pale and tired, and he walked with a limp.
He asked for wine, drank it quickly, and looked a little better.
He went upstairs to wash, and the guests whispered about him.
He came back clean and ate his dinner as if he were starving.
He said, “I will tell you everything, but please do not interrupt me.”
The Time Traveller said that he finished the machine that day.
He pushed the lever, and the room grew dim around him.
Night came after day, then day after night, faster and faster.
He felt sick, and he was afraid that the machine would crash.
The sun jumped across the sky, and the moon went round and round.
Soon the days were only a grey blur, and tall buildings came and went.
The little clocks on the machine turned fast, and a year passed every minute.
He was afraid of hitting something solid, so he decided to slow down.
He pulled the lever back, and the world began to slow down again.
Suddenly the machine fell over, and he flew through the air.
He stood up, wet and sore, in a storm of hail.
He saw a grey hill, a bush and a strange new world.
Through the storm, he saw a huge white statue with wings.
He looked up at its stone face, and he felt afraid.
The sky cleared, and he took the two levers out of the machine.
A small, beautiful person in a purple coat ran toward him.
Soon more small people came, and they stood around him in a circle.
They touched his sleeve and spoke softly, but he did not understand them.
He pointed at the sky and made a sound like thunder, and they laughed.
They put flowers around his neck and took him down the hill.
At the bottom of the hill, he saw a green valley and huge buildings.
Then he thought of his machine and ran back up the hill.
The machine was gone, and there was only a flat place on the grass.
Deep marks in the grass led him to the base of the statue.
He knocked on the bronze doors, and they sounded empty inside.
The little people looked uneasy, and they turned away from him politely.
He sat down in despair, but he still had the two levers.
That evening, they took him to a huge old hall with a tall doorway.
Inside the hall, he asked about his machine, but nobody understood him.
He pointed at things, and the little people told him their names.
The little people brought him fruit, and he saw that they ate nothing else.
The great buildings had huge halls, but no kitchens and no private rooms.
At night, all the little people slept together in the same big hall.
He saw no cows, horses or dogs, and nobody working in the fields.
The men and women looked almost the same, and they played like children.
He saw nobody old and nobody sick, and he wondered where they were.
He walked among the ruins, and saw that the old world was gone.
They got tired very quickly, and they could not listen for long.
He thought that a world with no danger had made them soft and weak.
That evening he made a theory about this world, but it was wrong.
A few days later, he went down to the river to swim.
A small woman fell into the deep water, but nobody helped her.
The Time Traveller jumped in, caught her and pulled her to the bank.
He brought her back to life, but the others watched without any worry.
She smiled, gave him flowers, and told him her name was Weena.
Weena stayed with him all day and taught him many words.
She liked him very much, and she followed him everywhere, like a child.
He drew his machine on the ground, but Weena looked afraid and said nothing.
Each morning he went to the white statue, but he never found his machine.
Every evening Weena hurried home before dark, and he wondered why.
Weena begged him to sleep inside, and she shook when the dark came.
One evening, he saw a pale, ghostly shape running across the grass.
On dark nights, the little people sat close together in the great hall.
He thought he saw bright eyes in the dark, but he was not sure.
He found round wells in the ground, and a deep noise came from them.
He dropped a flower down a well, and the warm air pulled it down.
Wells and towers stood in the valley and gave air to something below.
He lay down and listened, and he heard a steady beat like a machine.
Weena was very afraid of the wells, and she would not talk about them.
He wondered if another kind of person lived under the ground.
He took his matches, told Weena he would return, and went to a well.
He climbed over the stone edge and found metal steps in the wall.
He climbed down and down, his arms hurt, and the noise grew louder.
At the bottom, he was in a warm, dark tunnel, and the noise was loud.
Pale shapes moved in the dark around him, and he felt something close.
He lit a match and saw white creatures with huge eyes run away.
The match went out, and he felt cold, soft hands touch him.
He struck out with his fist, found the steps and started to climb.
A hand caught his foot, but he kicked it away and climbed on.
He climbed out with his last match gone, and lay in the sun, shaking.
In the sun, he knew the ghosts were real, and Weena called them Morlocks.
He drew two groups of people in the dust, one above and one below.
He thought that rich and poor people had grown into two kinds of beings.
The Morlocks still worked the machines and made the clothes for the people above.
He saw that the Morlocks came out at night, when the moon was dark.
He felt horror, because the little people were food for the Morlocks.
He knew the Morlocks had pulled his machine into the statue and below.
He pushed on the bronze doors again, but they would not open.
He remembered a huge green building far away, and he hoped to find weapons.
He decided to go there, and Weena said that she would go too.
They set out early, and no other little person came with them.
They crossed the river by an old broken bridge made of stone.
In the warm sun, Weena laughed and ran among the flowers.
They passed some wells, and Weena kept far away from every one.
Weena got tired, and he carried her on his shoulders across a stream.
At noon, they rested in the shade, and he watched the sun.
From a hill, he saw the huge green building very clearly.
They walked on toward it, and the sun began to sink.
At last they reached a huge broken wall of green tiles.
He saw that the sun was low, and they had little time.
Inside the palace was a huge gallery, quiet and thick with dust.
The hall held the bones of a giant animal, and Weena held his hand.
They walked past broken cases of stones, and he saw it was a museum.
He found shelves of books that had turned into brown flakes.
He passed old machines that were rusty and no use to him.
He looked for a weapon, but the swords and guns were all rust.
In a room of chemicals, he found camphor, which burns very well.
He found a tin of matches, and when he tried one, it lit.
He broke an iron bar from an old machine, and had a weapon.
Through a broken window, he saw the red sky, and they had to leave.
They left the palace at dusk, and he carried Weena across the plain.
They came to a thick forest, and the first stars came out.
He decided to go through the forest, and he carried Weena in.
He heard soft steps and whispers all around, and saw white shapes.
A hand touched his shoulder, and he hit it with the iron bar.
Weena was too tired to walk, and so was he.
He made a fire, and he gathered dry sticks in a small open place.
He lit the sticks, and the bright flames pushed back the whispers.
By the light of the fire, he saw many pale creatures nearby.
The fire caught the dry trees, and it began to spread very fast.
He woke Weena and lifted her, but the heat and noise drove them away.
Burning branches fell around them, and bright sparks filled the air.
The Morlocks ran blindly through the smoke, and he fought them off.
The smoke grew thick, and he coughed and lost his way.
Suddenly he knew that Weena was no longer with him.
He shouted her name into the smoke, but nobody answered.
The fire drove him from the forest, and he could not go back.
At dawn, he lay tired on the hillside, and the forest still burned.
He searched the burnt wood at dawn, but he found only ashes.
He sat alone in the ashes and knew he would never see her again.
He woke late, and he knew he must go back to the statue.
He walked through the valley, where the little people played as before.
He climbed the hill toward the white statue and wondered how to open it.
To his surprise, the bronze doors at the bottom of the statue were open.
Inside a small dark room, he saw his machine, safe and bright.
He thought it was a trap, but they could not use the machine.
He went in, and the doors closed behind him, and it was dark.
He lit a match and saw the machine and the Morlocks creeping close.
With shaking hands, he fitted the levers on while the Morlocks reached for him.
He pulled the lever, and a pale hand held the shaking machine.
He kicked the hand away, and the machine leaped forward in time.
He did not go back, because he wanted to see what came next.
The sun grew bigger and more red, and the sky grew dark.
He slowed the machine and stopped on a wide, empty beach.
A huge red sun filled the sky, and the sea was still.
A giant crab, as big as a table, came crawling toward him.
More crabs came, and their long arms touched the machine.
A feeler touched his sleeve, and he jumped into the saddle.
He pulled the lever, and the crabs were left behind on the beach.
He went on, many more years, into a darker and colder world.
He stopped again, thousands of years later, on a cold, quiet shore.
There was ice on the sea, frost on the rocks, and thin air.
He saw a round, dark thing, as big as a football, with long arms.
It was the only living thing that he saw, and it hopped slowly away.
A black shadow crossed the sun, and the light began to fade.
Snow began to fall, and the cold grew worse.
He felt sick and weak, and the dying world made him feel very alone.
He decided to go home, and he pushed the lever the other way.
He passed through the years he knew, and he saw his own hill again.
He arrived in his laboratory, and only a few hours had passed.
He sat on the machine and saw grass and mud on its frame.
He wondered if it was a dream, but he found two white flowers.
He walked to the dining room, heard his friends, and opened the door.
In the dining room, he finished his story and looked at his guests.
At last the Editor said, “What a pity you are not a writer!”
The Medical Man said it was a dream, and the host did not argue.
The Time Traveller put two strange white flowers on the table.
The Psychologist looked closely at the flowers, but he did not know their name.
The host took them to the workshop, where the machine stood, dirty and scratched.
The guests went home, and nobody knew what to believe, not even the narrator.
The next day, the narrator found the Time Traveller in a hurry.
He packed a camera and a bag, and said he would bring proof.
He said, “Back in half an hour,” and gave him the flowers.
He climbed into the saddle, waved, and the machine faded like a ghost.
The narrator waited for an hour, then until dark, but nobody came back.
The Thursday dinners went on, but the host's chair stayed empty.
Three years passed with no news, and the narrator wondered where he was.
He wondered if the story might be true of our own future.
He also thought that people can choose a kinder world.
He kept the flowers, and thought that kindness may live on, even in darkness.
B1B2: On Thursday evenings, a group of friends dine at the Time Traveller's house in Richmond, a small town near London. They are a lively company, and the narrator is one of them.
When dinner is over, the guests sit with their coffee and cigars while the host stands before the fire. His grey eyes shine as he asks them to be patient with a strange idea.

He begins with something that every schoolboy knows: a line drawn on paper has length but no thickness at all. A flat surface has length and breadth, he adds, but it has no thickness either, so neither of them can truly exist.
A cube that you can really touch needs three measures: length, breadth and thickness. Everybody agrees, the Time Traveller says, and everybody has always agreed that space has three dimensions.
Then Filby asks why there should not be a fourth dimension. The host smiles and replies that there is one, and that it is Time, because nothing real can exist without lasting for some time.

He asks them to imagine portraits of the same man at eight, fifteen, seventeen and twenty-three years old. Each portrait, he says, is a slice of one long being, whose fourth measure is the length of his life.
The Psychologist objects that we can move about freely in space, but nobody can move about in time. The host answers that this is exactly where people are mistaken.
When we remember something vividly, he says, we jump back to that moment for a short while. A balloon lets a man rise above the ground, he says, so one day he may stop, or turn back, in time.

Some of the guests laugh, and the Medical Man says that it is a clever joke and nothing more. Filby shakes his head and demands proof, because he will not accept a thing only because it is argued well.

The Time Traveller answers calmly that he is not joking and that he has worked on this idea for years. He asks them to wait a moment, then leaves the room, and the guests look at one another in surprise.

After a few minutes, the Time Traveller returns carrying a small and delicate machine, no bigger than a carriage clock. It is made of brass and ivory, with bars of clear crystal that shine in the lamplight.

The guests pass it from hand to hand, and the Psychologist turns it over to look for hidden wires. The host tells them that it is a model of a machine for travelling through time, and that it is quite real.
He shows them two small levers on the model, and he explains what each of them does. One sends the machine gliding into the future, he says, and the other makes it go back the way it came.
He asks the Psychologist to check the table, so that nobody can say there is any trick. Then he presses the lever, and the little machine trembles, grows faint like a ghost, and vanishes.
For a moment nobody speaks, and every guest simply stares at the empty place under the lamp. The Psychologist gets down on his knees to look under the table, but he finds nothing there at all.

The Time Traveller laughs and says that the machine has not been destroyed, because it has simply gone into time. It is in the same place as before, he explains, but moving so fast that no eye can catch it.

The Medical Man says that this is a clever piece of conjuring, and Filby wants to see more. The host takes a lamp and leads some of them down the passage to his laboratory, where a bigger machine waits.
The narrator walks around the machine and sees that its parts are still unfinished. There is brass, ivory and shining nickel everywhere, and bars of clear quartz stand ready beside the saddle.
On the workbench lie many drawings, covered with careful numbers and notes. The Time Traveller says that the machine will be ready by next week, and that he means to explore time himself.
Filby asks him whether he will go into the past or the future, but the host cannot say. The guests walk home through the cold night, and none of them is sure what to believe.
The next Thursday, the narrator arrives at the house in Richmond and finds a dozen men already in the hall. The Time Traveller himself is nowhere to be seen, and his chair stands empty.
The Medical Man is standing by the fire, and he reads out a note that the host has left for them. It says that he has been delayed, and that they should begin dinner at seven without him.
The Editor of a well-known newspaper says it would be a pity to let the food spoil, so the bell is rung. The guests sit down, and soon they are talking about the little machine that vanished.
The Editor and the Journalist think that the whole thing was a trick, and they laugh at the story. The narrator tries to explain what he has seen, but he finds that it is hard to make it sound true.
The Medical Man is making a joke about it, when the door opens very quietly at the end of the room. The narrator is facing it, and he is the first to see the figure standing there.

It is the Time Traveller, but he looks like a tramp, with a dusty coat, stained with green and brown. His hair is greyer than before, his face is as white as paper, and there is a half-healed cut on his chin.
He limps into the room and holds out his hand for a glass of wine. He drinks it down in one gulp, and some colour returns to his face, as if the wine has woken him.
He tells them that he is quite all right, and that he is going upstairs to wash and change. They must save him some mutton, he adds, because he is starving, and then he climbs the stairs slowly.

The guests whisper to one another, and the Doctor wonders aloud whether somebody has hurt him. When the host returns, he is dressed in a clean coat, but his eyes are still wild, and he eats very hungrily.

After dinner they go to the fire, where the Time Traveller sits in his deep armchair and lights a pipe. He says that he will tell them everything, but only if nobody interrupts, and the guests all agree.
The Time Traveller tells them that he finished the machine that very day. He checks every screw once more, puts a drop of oil on the quartz rod, and sits down in the saddle.
He takes the starting lever in one hand and pushes it, and the laboratory grows hazy and dim. His housekeeper, Mrs Watchett, walks across the room without seeing him, as fast as a rabbit.
He pulls the lever as far as it will go, and night comes like a lamp being turned out. In a moment tomorrow has come, and then another night, and another day, faster and faster.
He cannot explain how strange the feeling is, but it is like a headlong fall on a switchback. All the time he is afraid that something terrible is about to happen.
The laboratory seems to fall away from him, and he sees the sun hop across the sky once every minute. The moon runs through its quarters, and the stars wheel overhead.
Soon the days and nights merge into a grey blur, and the sky turns a deep, shining blue. The sun is a streak of fire, trees grow and vanish like puffs of steam, and tall buildings rise like dreams.

The little dials on the machine spin faster and faster, and he sees the sun swing between summer and winter in less than a minute. White snow flashes across the world, and then the bright green of spring.

Then a terrible thought strikes him: what if the machine stops in a place where something solid stands? Its atoms would mix with the atoms of the object, and the result might be a huge explosion, so he decides to slow down.
He pulls hard on the lever, and the grey blur begins to slow. The ghostly shapes become solid again, the sun crawls, and the hills grow clear as the machine comes towards the end of its journey.
But he is too hasty in stopping, and the machine pitches forward like a horse that has stumbled. He is thrown through the air and lands on his hands and knees in soft grass.
The Time Traveller sits up and finds himself wet, bruised and shaking, in the middle of a fierce hailstorm. The machine lies on its side behind him, and the hail dances like smoke over the grass.

As the hail slowly thins, he looks about at a grey, rolling hillside, with a big rhododendron bush shining with water. Nothing is as he remembers, and he understands that the world has changed greatly.
Through the grey rain he sees a giant statue, which rises high above him on a bronze pedestal. It is a white sphinx with its wings lifted, and its face is pitted by wind and rain, as if it is ill.
The stone eyes seem to watch him, and he thinks that he can see a faint smile on the face. A cold fear grows in him, for he wonders what kind of people now live in this strange world.
Because he is afraid of thieves, he pulls the machine upright, unscrews its two levers and puts them in his pocket. Without the levers, nobody will be able to make it move, and he can still escape.

The storm ends, and a small figure comes running down the path towards him, wearing a purple tunic tied with a leather belt. This person is about four feet tall, with bare legs, curling hair and a face of delicate, almost unreal beauty.
Soon five or six more arrive, all dressed in the same soft way, and they gather round him in a circle. They are beautiful and graceful, but they look frail, as if a strong wind could break them.
They are not afraid of him, and one of them reaches out and touches his sleeve, then his hand. They speak together in sweet, soft voices, but he cannot understand a word of what they say.
To test them, he points at the sky and makes a noise like thunder, hoping to ask about the storm. They only stare at him with big eyes, and then two or three of them laugh like children.
They bring flowers from the bushes and hang them around his neck, and the sweet smell makes him a little dizzy. Then, laughing and chattering, they take him by the hand and lead him down the hill.

At the foot of the hill, he sees a wide green valley full of flowering bushes and huge, strange buildings. He notices that there are no fences, no hedges and no farms, and that nobody seems to be working.
Suddenly he thinks of the Time Machine, left alone on the hilltop, and he feels a stab of fear. He turns and runs back up the hill, and the little people follow him, laughing as if it were a game.
When he reaches the sphinx, the machine is gone, and there is only a flat patch of grass where it lay. For a moment he cannot think or move, because he knows that his only way home has disappeared.

He looks closely at the ground and finds long, deep marks in the wet turf, which run straight to the bronze pedestal. He searches wildly around the statue and in all the bushes, but he finds nothing at all.

The pedestal has two bronze panels, set into the side like doors, with no handle or keyhole. He raps on them with his fist and hears a hollow sound, and he begins to think that something is hidden inside.

The little people do not like what he is doing, and they make small, anxious signs for him to stop. When he looks at them, they turn away politely, like people who do not want to see someone else's mistake.
