The Psychologist, recovering first, knelt down and looked beneath the table with the stern face of a man searching for a lost coin. Of course he found nothing at all, and he rose slowly to his feet again, a little pink in the face.

The Time Traveller laughed with pleasure and told them that the machine had not been destroyed, but had merely gone into time. It still stood in the very same place, he said, but it was travelling through the days so quickly that the eye could not catch it, much as a spinning wheel seems to be still. Whether it had gone into the past or the future, he confessed, he could not say.

The Medical Man observed that it was an admirable piece of conjuring, and Filby, still unwilling to be won over, said that he would like to see more. Taking a lamp in his hand, the host led them down a long passage to his laboratory, a low and silent building behind the house. There, among the shadows, stood another machine, many times larger than the first, and plainly built for the same strange purpose.

The narrator walked slowly around it, noticing that it was still unfinished, and that parts of the frame lay unfastened on the floor. There was brass and ivory everywhere, and shining nickel, and slender rods of clear quartz had been laid ready beside a small, plain saddle. He touched one of the bars, and it was cool and smooth, and quite real.

On the workbench were drawings in pencil, covered with careful figures and notes, and the guests understood that years of thought lay behind them. The Time Traveller said that the machine would be finished by the end of the week, and that he meant to use it. Then, with his eyes shining, he declared that he intended to explore time itself, and he looked as calm as a man who is going on a short holiday.

The Medical Man asked whether he would go into the past or into the future, and the host said that he could not tell, since he would have to find out when he got there. The guests took their leave and walked home through the cold streets, conversing in low and doubtful voices. The narrator reflected that the Time Traveller was one of those men whose cleverness makes them hard to credit, and that no one present had yet reached a verdict.

On the following Thursday the narrator walked up to the house in Richmond at the usual hour, and found a dozen men already waiting in the hall. The Time Traveller himself was nowhere to be seen, and the great chair at the head of the table stood empty. It seemed an odd thing, since he was ordinarily the most punctual of hosts and had never before kept his friends waiting.

The Medical Man stood by the fire with a folded paper in his hand, and he read out the note that their host had left behind. It said that he had been unavoidably delayed, and that his friends should begin dinner at seven without him, as he would explain everything when he returned. Nobody in the hall could guess what the delay might be, and the narrator felt a faint stir of unease at the thought.

The Editor of a well-known daily paper remarked that it would be a pity to let a good dinner spoil, and the Doctor rang the bell. The guests took their seats, with one place left bare, and as the soup went round the conversation turned at once to the little machine that had vanished from the table. Every man had a theory, and each theory was more confident than the last.

The Editor and the Journalist thought that the whole affair was nothing but conjuring, and they laughed over it until the narrator felt obliged to speak up. He said that he had seen the model with his own eyes, and that he could not account for it, but he found it difficult to make the story sound true. Even to himself, in that warm and ordinary room, it seemed rather less likely than it had the week before.

The Medical Man was in the middle of a joke about travellers who lose their luggage in the fourth dimension, when the door at the far end of the room opened without a sound. The narrator sat facing it, and so he was the first to see who stood there. He cried out a greeting of surprise and relief, and the others turned in their chairs to see what had startled him.

It was the Time Traveller, but he looked as if he had walked a hundred miles in the rain, for his coat was dusty and smeared with green and brown, and his hair was greyer than before. His face was ghastly pale, and across his chin there was a brown cut, half healed, while his expression was that of a man who has suffered greatly. He stood for a moment in the doorway, blinking as though dazzled by the light and unsure of where he was.

He limped across the room like a footsore tramp, and the narrator saw that his socks were stained with blood. Without a word, he took a glass of wine from the table and drank it off, and some colour came back into his cheeks. A faint ghost of his old smile flickered across his face, and he looked about him at the astonished company.

He told them that he was perfectly all right, and that they were not to let him disturb their dinner. He would go upstairs to wash and change, he said, but meanwhile they must save him some mutton, for he was starving. Then he climbed the stairs slowly, and the guests sat listening in puzzled silence to his uneven step overhead.

The guests exchanged glances, and the Doctor wondered in a whisper whether he had been attacked on the road, while the Editor muttered that it was all very mysterious. When the Time Traveller came down again, he was dressed in a clean dinner coat and looked almost himself. Yet his eyes held something wild and far away, and he ate with the fierce hunger of a man who has gone without food for days.

After the meal they gathered around the fire, and the Time Traveller sank into his deep armchair, lit a pipe and sat for a while looking at the flames. At last he said that he would tell them the whole story, but that it would sound like a lie, and he asked that nobody should break in upon it. When the guests agreed, one after another, he took his pipe from his lips and began.

The Time Traveller told them that the machine had been finished that very day, and that he had gone over every screw once more, oiled the quartz rod and sat himself down in the saddle. He remembered that his hand was trembling, though he could not have said whether it was fear or excitement. Then, with a long breath, he reached for the lever that would begin the journey.

He pushed the starting lever gently, and at once the laboratory grew hazy and dim, like a room seen through steam. Mrs Watchett, his housekeeper, came in and walked across the floor towards the garden door, quite blind to him, and so swift that she seemed to flash by like a rabbit. He understood that to her he had already vanished, and a cold thrill went through him.

Then he pulled the lever over to its extreme position, and the night came like the turning out of a lamp, and in another moment tomorrow had come. Tomorrow's night followed, black as ink, and then day again, and night again, and day, faster and faster still. A confused murmur filled his ears, and a strange dumbness settled upon his mind.

He confessed that the sensations of travelling in time are excessively unpleasant, and he could not convey them to his audience. They are like the feelings of a man on a switchback, a helpless rush forward, accompanied by the dreadful certainty that a smash is at hand. As the pace increased, night followed day like the flapping of a great black wing.

The faint outline of the laboratory seemed to drop away, and he saw the sun hopping across the sky, leaping the whole arc every minute, and every minute marking a day. The moon spun swiftly through her quarters, from new to full, and now and then he caught a glimpse of the circling stars. He supposed that the laboratory had been destroyed, and that he was out in the open air.

As he gained speed, the throbbing of night and day merged into one continuous greyness, and the sky took on a wonderful depth of blue, like the colour of early twilight. The jerking sun became a streak of fire and the moon a fainter, flickering band, while trees grew and changed like puffs of vapour. Huge buildings rose up, faint and fair, and passed away like dreams, and the whole surface of the earth seemed to melt and flow beneath his eyes.

The little hands on the dials that recorded his speed raced round faster and faster, and soon he saw that the sun's path swung up and down from solstice to solstice in less than a minute. That meant that his pace was more than a year a minute, and minute by minute the white snow flashed across the world, and vanished, and was followed by the bright, brief green of spring. He gripped the saddle with both hands, and for a time he could think of nothing at all, not even of his fear.

Then a new fear came upon him, for he remembered that matter might stand where the machine would stop, and that atoms of metal and atoms of stone cannot share the same place. If they tried to do so, there would be a chemical reaction, perhaps a monstrous explosion, and the traveller and his machine would be thrown out of every possible dimension. He had known this when he started, but only now did he feel it, and he resolved to stop.

In a kind of mad despair he dragged the lever back, and the world seemed to wake from a dream and grow solid around him. The hands on the dials slowed, the flicker of night and day became less and less, and the ghosts of hills and trees grew firm. He had a glimpse of a grey and rolling country, with the sky above it dark and heavy with cloud.

But he was clumsy in his haste, and the machine stopped abruptly, pitching forward like a horse that has missed its footing. The traveller was shot out of the saddle and flung through the air, and he came down with a crash upon soft turf, a few paces from the fallen machine. For a second he lay there without moving, with his heart pounding and the whole world swimming around him.

The traveller sat up on the soft turf, bruised and breathless, with the hail rattling on his head and shoulders and dancing like smoke over the grass. The machine lay on its side a few yards away, and for a moment he did nothing but stare at it. Then he rose unsteadily to his feet, drenched and shivering, and looked about him.

The rain had begun to thin, and through it he made out a grey and rolling hillside, scattered with bushes, among which a huge rhododendron shone with the water that ran from its leaves. Nothing was as he remembered it, and nothing, he realised with a shock, was in the least familiar. The world had changed, and he was the only thing in it that had not.

As the greyness thinned, a colossal figure loomed up out of it, carved in some white stone and raised on a high pedestal of bronze. It was a sphinx, with its wings lifted as though it were about to rise from the ground, and its face was worn and pitted by the wind and rain of centuries. The whole thing had a diseased look, and it seemed to him almost unbearable to look at.

The stone eyes appeared to watch him, and he fancied that he could see on its lips a faint and mocking smile. A sudden panic seized him, and for a moment he felt like a lost child in a vast and unfriendly place. He wondered what sort of men might live in this age, and what they might have become, and whether they would be cruel.

With the first return of his courage, he went back to the machine, set it upright with a great effort, and then did something that seemed prudent. He unscrewed the two small levers that made it move, and put them carefully in his pocket, so that no one could ride away on it and leave him stranded. As he did so, the last of the clouds broke, and the sun came out upon the hill.

Then, along a path through the wet grass, he saw a small figure running towards him, clad in a purple tunic girdled at the waist with a leather belt. It was a creature about four feet high, with bare legs, a bare head of curling hair and a face of delicate, almost unreal beauty. There was a hectic, fragile prettiness about it, like the flush that one sees on the cheek of a sick child.

Others appeared behind it, five or six in all, and they came up laughing and chattering and made a ring around him. All of them were dressed in the same soft, bright robes, and all had the same slight frames and the same lovely and frail faces. They did not seem in any way afraid of him, which surprised him very much.

One of them stepped forward and touched his sleeve, and then very gently his hand, as though to make sure that he was real. They spoke among themselves in a soft, liquid language, sweet and musical to the ear, but he could not understand a single word of it. He tried to answer, and they listened with their heads on one side, like children listening to a stranger.

Hoping to learn something about the storm, he pointed at the sky and made a rumbling noise like thunder, accompanying it with a gesture. They looked at him with wide, puzzled eyes, and then two or three of them burst out laughing, with a pretty, careless laughter. He felt oddly foolish, and he had the first suspicion that there was something childlike in their minds.

They gathered flowers from the bushes beside the path, and they hung them around his neck, until he was sweet with the scent of them and almost faint. Then, still laughing, they took him by the hands and began to lead him down the hill, as if they had been expecting a guest. He went with them willingly enough, for in that strange and silent country he could think of nothing better to do.

At the foot of the hill, the whole valley lay spread out before him, green and golden in the returning sun, and dotted with huge buildings of strange design. There were flowering bushes everywhere, but no fences, no hedges, no fields and no signs of farming. It looked more like an enormous garden than a country where people had to earn their bread.

Suddenly he thought of the machine, left alone on the hilltop with no one to guard it, and a pang of fear went through him. He turned about and ran back up the slope, and the little people followed, laughing and calling to one another as though he had invited them to a game. Not one of them seemed to guess what troubled him, and he had no words with which to explain.

When he reached the sphinx, he saw at once that the machine was gone, and that only a flat patch of crushed grass showed where it had lain. For a long moment he could neither think nor move, for the whole meaning of it struck him like a blow. His only road home had vanished, and he had been robbed within an hour of his arrival.

Kneeling, he examined the ground and found two long, deep furrows in the wet turf, as though something heavy had been dragged along it. The marks ran straight towards the pedestal of the sphinx, and he followed them, and then searched wildly round the statue and through every bush on the hill. He found nothing at all, and the little people looked on throughout with the mild curiosity of children watching a stranger.

The bronze pedestal had two great panels set into its side, like doors, but they had neither handle nor keyhole to be seen. He rapped upon them with his fist, and they gave out a hollow sound, which told him plainly that there was a space behind them. The conviction came to him that his machine was lying inside, though he could not imagine how it had got there.

The little people did not like his knocking, for they made small, anxious signs which he took to mean that he should stop. When he turned and stared at them, they dropped their eyes and looked away with a delicate politeness, like well-bred people who have noticed a stranger's blunder. There was something in their manner that he could not explain, and it troubled him.

At last he sat down on the grass and put his head in his hands, feeling very small and very far from the warm, familiar world of the Thursday dinners. Then, quite by chance, his fingers closed on the levers in his pocket, and a ray of hope came to him. Whoever had taken the machine could not make it move, since the means of moving it were still in his keeping.

As evening drew on, the little people took him by the hands and led him to a huge hall of grey stone with a vast carved doorway, weathered by uncounted winters. It was a ruin in places, with tiles fallen from the roof and walls cracked and stained, yet it was still grand, and plainly built to hold hundreds of people. He passed under the arch and felt as though he had stepped into a cathedral.

Inside, the little people made a circle round him on the cushions that lay about the floor, and he tried once more to ask where his machine might have gone. They smiled and glanced at each other and answered him in their sweet, bird-like voices, but he saw at once that they understood nothing of what he wanted. It was a strange and frightening thing to be so alone among so many friendly faces.

So he made up his mind to learn their language, and he began by pointing at things in the hall and waiting for them to say the names aloud. They took to the game with pleasure, repeating each word and laughing at his clumsy attempts, but they were easily distracted. Before long their attention wandered, and they lost all interest in the lesson, like children who have grown tired of a toy.

The little people brought him fruit in great quantity, a large three-sided kind with a rough brown rind and sweet pink flesh, and he ate it gladly after his long journey. He discovered, over the following days, that fruit was the only food they ever touched, and that they never ate meat, bread or anything cooked. Being hungry and tired, he did not at first stop to reflect how very odd this was for a whole people.

He explored the huge buildings and saw that, for all their grandeur, they contained halls and passages but no kitchens, no fireplaces and no separate rooms for families or individuals. Everything seemed to be shared, as though the whole people were a single household, with no one possessing anything of his own. There were no signs of shops or workshops, no coins and no markets, and not the faintest trace of any sort of trade.

When night fell, all the little people lay down together in the great halls, in long rows upon the cushions, and slept in their dozens like children in a school dormitory. Nobody ever slept alone, and the traveller, curious but tired, assumed that this was merely a habit of their communal life. Only much later did he understand what lay behind it, and he shuddered at his own blindness.

He wandered across the valley and noticed that there were no cows, no sheep, no horses and no dogs, and not a single labourer in all the fields that he could see. He looked for tools, and for the sheds and barns of a farming people, and found nothing at all. It struck him that all the creatures which had once served man seemed to have vanished from the earth.

The men and women resembled one another closely, being of the same small size, wearing the same soft clothes and having the same delicate, rather feminine faces. They played and laughed like children, ran after butterflies and threw flowers at each other, and he could not tell the young from the old. In all that time he did not see a single serious or troubled face.

He looked for the old and the sick, as one does in any country, and he saw neither, which made him wonder where such people were kept. Perhaps the little people did not grow old, or perhaps disease had been conquered altogether, he thought; but this seemed too good to be true. Something in the whole arrangement left him uneasy, though he could not name it.

On his walks, he came upon huge ruins of grey granite, with roofs fallen in and walls cracked from top to bottom, and weeds growing thickly in every crevice. They were the bones of a great city, he guessed, and they told him that this beautiful quiet world had grown out of a much larger and busier one. Nobody now lived in them, and no one even seemed to look at them.

He soon found that the little people had hardly any strength and hardly any patience, and could not give their attention to anything for more than a minute or two. In the midst of a game or a conversation they would yawn, stretch themselves upon the grass and fall asleep, as though the effort of being awake had exhausted them. He found it at once touching and a little frightening, like watching a candle that could not stay lit.

Sitting for hours on the hillside, he thought long about all that he had seen, and he arrived at an explanation that pleased him greatly. In a world with no danger, no hardship and no enemy, he reasoned, neither strength of body nor sharpness of mind had any use, and so both had slowly faded away. Man had conquered nature, and in the very hour of his victory he had lost the qualities that had won it.

As the sun set over the peaceful valley and the sky turned crimson behind the ruins, he named his idea the sunset of mankind and felt rather proud of it. It explained the idle people, the empty fields and the silence of the great houses, and it seemed to him a very reasonable theory. He did not yet know that it was only half the truth, and that the other half was waiting for him in the dark.

Some days later, having begun to feel at home in the valley, the Time Traveller walked down to the river Thames to bathe. Several of the little people went with him and settled lazily on the bank, in the warm sun, while the water ran smooth and green. In the middle of the stream the current was swift and deep, and he took care to keep to the shallows.

One of the small women, who had been playing at the water's edge, slipped suddenly into the deep part and was caught by the current. She was carried quickly away, with her thin arms raised and her mouth open in a faint, helpless cry, and the others, sitting on the bank, merely watched her go. Not one of them moved or called out, as if the matter were of no importance.

He threw off his coat and dived into the river, and a few strong strokes brought him up with the drowning girl, whom he seized in his arms. The current dragged at them both, but he was a good swimmer, and he fought his way back to the bank, where he laid her down on the grass. She was limp and cold, and for a moment he feared that he had come too late.

Kneeling over her, he rubbed her hands and turned her gently, as he had once been taught, until at last she coughed, sighed and began to breathe again. He looked up and saw the others standing in a loose ring, regarding the scene with a mild, vague curiosity. It horrified him that nobody showed alarm or gratitude, and he began to suspect that these people felt very little at all.

When she had recovered, the small woman sat up, gazed at him with her wide, grave eyes and took his hand and kissed it. Then she ran to the bushes, gathered armfuls of flowers and filled his pockets with them, laughing, and he understood that this was her way of saying thank you. He learned that her name was Weena, and the word seemed to him as soft and sweet as herself.

Weena stayed by him the whole of that day and proved to be a patient teacher, repeating each word slowly until he had it right. By the evening he knew the names of a good many objects, and the verbs for eating, sleeping and walking, and he could put together a few clumsy sentences. It gave him a pleasure out of all proportion to the little he had learned.

She grew very fond of him, and wherever he went she followed, holding his hand like a younger sister and chattering in her musical voice. He was touched and a little embarrassed, because her kindness seemed deeper and more truly felt than the careless good humour of the rest. In all that dreamy valley, she was the only one who seemed to him to have a heart.

One afternoon he drew a picture of his machine in the dust, with the saddle and the levers, and tried to ask her where it might have gone. Weena looked at the drawing for a moment, then looked away, and her pretty face went pale, as though the question had frightened her badly. She would say nothing whatever about it, and he did not like to press her while she looked so unhappy.

Every morning he climbed the hill to the white sphinx and examined its bronze doors, hoping to discover some hidden catch or spring. He found none, and the little people who came to watch him did so with polite and empty smiles, as one watches a child at a puzzle. The days passed, and the machine remained as far from him as the year he had left.

At sunset Weena always took his hand and begged him, in her soft broken words, to come back to the great hall before the dark. He agreed, because he liked to please her, but he could not help wondering what she feared. It seemed strange to him that a girl who would not turn her head for a drowning companion should tremble at the coming of night.

Each night Weena begged him to sleep in the great hall, among the others, and as soon as the light began to fade she would take his hand and tremble like a leaf. He tried gently to find out what troubled her, but her small vocabulary and her terror together made it impossible. She would say only a word that he did not know and then hide her face against his sleeve.

One evening, as the last light was draining from the valley, he caught sight of a pale and ghostly shape running across the grass at the edge of the trees. It moved very quickly, crouched low and, as it seemed to him, on all fours, and before he could study it properly it had plunged into a thicket and vanished. He told himself that it was only the dusk playing tricks with his eyes.

On the darkest nights, when there was no moon at all, the little people drew together into the great halls and clung to one another in the blackness, wide-eyed and silent. He had not noticed it clearly before, but now he saw how deeply they dreaded the dark, and how the whole of their carefree life seemed to shrink and tighten as soon as the sun went down. It struck him as a strange fear for a world that was supposed to have no enemies.

Late one evening, among the shadows of a ruined building, he fancied that he saw a pair of eyes gleaming with a greenish light, like those of a cat. He blinked, and they were gone, and he told himself severely that it was only the strain of his loneliness and the strangeness of his position. Even so, a coldness stayed with him, and he went back to the hall earlier than usual.

As he explored further, he began to notice round wells scattered about the valley, each with a low stone rim and a deep black mouth that seemed to go down for ever. From these openings there rose a dull, regular thudding, which he had never heard in the open air, and which seemed far too powerful to come from any natural cause. He stood there for a long time, listening, with the sun warm on his back.

He picked one of Weena's white flowers from his pocket and let it fall into the nearest well, and it did not drop as a stone would drop. Instead it drifted slowly out of sight, as if a current of warm air were rising from below and drawing it gently down into the darkness. Somewhere under his feet, he realised with a small shiver, there was a deep place that breathed like a living thing.

He found more wells as he walked, and beside some of them stood tall, narrow towers that rose from the grass like factory chimneys, with a shimmer of heated air about their tops. It occurred to him that they must be ventilating shafts, bringing air to some great hidden place under the earth. The idea was so strange that he laughed aloud, although he was quite alone.

Lying on his stomach beside one of the wells, he laid his ear against the cold stone rim, and listened for a long time to the sound that came up from the depths. It was a steady, heavy pulse, like the beating of a great heart, or of enormous machines that had been working in the dark since the beginning of time. He felt it through his ribs and the soles of his feet as much as he heard it with his ears.

When he asked Weena about the wells, she turned deathly pale, shook her head and would not so much as look at them, even from a distance. He saw that the other little people avoided those places too, passing them in a wide circle, and not one of them could be coaxed into saying what lay below. Their silence, he thought, told him more about the place below than any answer could have done.

That evening he sat on the hillside and watched the sun sinking behind the wells and the towers, and a new and disturbing thought began to take shape in his mind. Perhaps there was another race beneath the ground, he reasoned, a people who tended the machines and kept the whole apparatus of the world running for the idle folk above. If so, then his beautiful theory of mankind at rest was only a small part of a much larger and darker picture.

Early one morning, determined to learn the truth for himself, he put a box of matches in his pocket and walked to the nearest well. Weena ran after him, clung to his arm and begged him in a voice full of tears not to go. He kissed her forehead, promised that he would return before noon, and gently freed himself from her small, trembling hands.

At the edge of the well he looked down into the black shaft, and saw that a row of metal rungs ran down the side, rusted but still firm. He took a deep breath, swung his legs over the stone rim, tested the first rung with his foot and began to climb down into the dark. Above him the sky was blue and warm, and below him lay something that no man of his own age had ever seen.

The round patch of daylight above grew smaller and smaller, until it was no larger than a coin, while the thudding of the machines below grew louder with every rung. His arms began to ache and his hands to slip, and the air became warmer and heavier, with a faint, unpleasant smell that he could not name. He told himself that he was a fool, and went on downward all the same.

At last his foot met solid ground, and he found himself standing at the mouth of a low tunnel that ran away into total darkness. The noise of the machines was tremendous now, a deep and ceaseless pounding that he could feel through the soles of his boots and in the stone against his palm. He stood very still, with his heart beating hard, and waited for his eyes to grow used to the gloom.

Slowly he began to make out pale shapes moving at the edge of his vision, and something stirred very close to him in the dark, with a quick and furtive sound of breathing. It was not Weena's breathing, nor that of any of her gentle people, and the hair rose on the back of his neck. He fumbled in his pocket for the matches, and his hand was shaking so that he nearly dropped the box.

He struck a match, and the little flame jumped up and showed him, for an instant, a crowd of white, ghastly creatures, with long arms, wide grey-red eyes and a pelt of pale hair upon their heads. They were like apes and yet like men, and they shrank from the light, covering their faces and blinking as though it hurt them. He realised that these were the owners of the thudding, and that they had lived in the dark for a very long time.

The match burned down to his fingers and went out, and the darkness that followed seemed blacker than any he had known. Then he felt a cold, soft hand upon his sleeve, and another upon his neck, and he knew that the creatures were creeping close to him again, now that the light was gone. He had been, he understood too late, a very rash and foolish explorer, and he had no idea how he would get back.

With a cry of horror he lashed out at them with his fist, and the blow landed on something soft that squealed and fell back. Then he turned, groped along the wall for the rungs and found them, and began to climb with the frantic speed of a man whose life depends on every foot. He could hear them close behind him, scrabbling and whispering in the dark, and he did not dare to look down.

Halfway up the shaft a hand seized his ankle in a grip that was cold, damp and surprisingly strong, and for a dreadful moment he thought that it would drag him down. He kicked blindly with his free foot, felt his boot strike something yielding, heard a thin cry of pain, and felt the hand loosen and fall away. Then he climbed on, gasping, with his heart hammering and the creatures' voices slowly dwindling in the darkness below him.

At length he reached the top and heaved himself over the rim, with his hands torn, his knees bruised and his last match long gone. He lay on his back in the grass, blinking up at the blazing sky and shaking from head to foot, while Weena came running across the lawn with a cry of relief. She threw herself down beside him and caught his hand, and for a long time neither of them spoke.

Lying in the sunshine, with his heart slowly quieting, he knew beyond any doubt that the pale shapes were no ghosts, and Weena, weeping and clinging to his arm, spoke a word that he now understood. They were Morlocks, she whispered, and her face was full of dread as she said it. Nothing, he realised, had ever frightened her people so deeply as these creatures of the dark.

With a twig he drew two groups in the dust, one above a line and one below it, and he began to puzzle out how two kinds of men might have drifted apart over the ages. His own age, he reflected, had already shown the first signs of such a split. The thought was one that he did not like at all, and yet he could not drive it away.

In the nineteenth century, he reminded himself, the rich had already enjoyed the sunlight and the fresh air, while the poor had already worked in smoky, crowded places underground. If that gulf between the two had widened without limit, century after century, the rich would at last have lived entirely on the surface, and the workers entirely beneath it. Each would then, over the ages, have changed in body and in mind to suit the home that it had been given.

The Morlocks, he supposed, must still tend the machines that kept the world running, and probably made the soft clothes that the people on the surface wore. For some time he believed that they were no more than servants, hidden away because the idle folk above preferred not to see the work done for them. It seemed to him a dreary arrangement, but not a terrible one, and he thought no more about it for a while.

Then the truth began to dawn on him, for he remembered that the pale creatures came up from the wells at night, and that this was why the little people feared the dark. The terror was worst when the moon was gone, because then the Morlocks could creep about the valley without being seen. It explained why the little people slept together, and why they never slept alone.

He lay awake beside sleeping Weena, listening to the quiet night, and a dreadful thought took shape in his mind. The little people were fed and clothed and sheltered, and they never worked, and they lived without a care, which was precisely how one treats cattle. The Morlocks were keeping them for food, and the gentle world above was nothing more than a pasture.

He thought of the long furrows in the grass, and suddenly everything fitted together, like the pieces of a puzzle laid out on a table. The Morlocks had taken his machine, dragged it up to the sphinx and carried it through the bronze doors, which must open on a passage to the world below. The great statue, which he had taken for a monument, was really a door, and the doorkeeper was watching him.

He climbed to the sphinx once more and threw his whole weight against the bronze panels, but they were as firm as the rock itself. He knocked and called, and nobody answered, though he could almost feel a pair of great eyes behind the metal, listening and waiting. He went away angry and ashamed, and he knew that he would need some other way.

As the evening light spread across the valley, he remembered something that he had glimpsed from the hilltops in his first few days. Far off to the north-west there stood a huge building, whose walls shone with a greenish gleam like china, and he thought that it might be a museum or a palace. If any weapons of the old age had survived the centuries, he thought, they were most likely to be found there.

He resolved to go there at once, since he could not hope to face the Morlocks with nothing but his bare hands. Weena, who had followed him through the whole of the day with her small, anxious face, filled a basket with fruit and declared that she was coming too. He tried to argue, but she looked at him with such gentle stubbornness that at last he gave way.

They left early the next morning, while the dew was still on the grass, and set out on the long walk to the green building. The other little people waved goodbye with sleepy smiles, as if the departure were nothing more than a game, and not one of them offered to come. He noticed it with a pang, but he did not blame them, for he knew what they were afraid of.

They crossed the river by the ruins of an old stone bridge, whose broken arches stood in the water like the teeth of some great jaw. He found himself wondering how many thousands of people had crossed it in the days of its use, and what crowds of carriages and trains and voices had once filled the valley. Now the only sound was the water, running under the broken arches as it had always run, with no one to hear it.

In the warm sun, Weena forgot her fears and ran ahead through the flowers, laughing and chasing the butterflies with her little hands. Shadows of white clouds slid across the grass in long slow waves, and for an hour or two the world seemed as gentle and lovely as a picture in a book. The Time Traveller watched her and thought that he had never seen anyone so happy.

Several times on the way they passed the black mouth of a well, with its low rim and its faint breath of warm air, and each time Weena made a wide circle around it. He noticed how many there were, far more than he had guessed, scattered across the plain like holes in a piece of cloth. He felt as though the whole country were hollow underneath him, and that the crust of it might break at any step.

After some hours, Weena grew tired, and her small legs began to drag, so he lifted her up onto his shoulders and carried her across a shallow stream. She held his head with both arms and sang softly to herself in her unknown language, and the weight of her was so slight that he hardly felt it. It was a strange thing to be so far from his own century and yet so tenderly cared for.

At noon they rested in the shade of a tree and ate fruit from the basket, and he leaned against the trunk and looked up at the sun. He could not help counting the hours of light that remained and measuring them against the miles that still lay before them. The sunlight was their only shield, he knew, and it was beginning to feel very short.

He climbed a low hill and looked out over a wide green plain, and there, much nearer than before, stood the building that he had seen from afar. It was vast and ruined, with towers fallen and walls cracked, yet its outer wall still shone with a greenish gleam, like old china in the sun. It was by far the largest thing that he had yet seen in all this strange and silent world.

They walked on towards it for what seemed a very long time, and the great ruin grew larger and larger until it filled half the sky. The sun, however, grew lower and lower, and long blue shadows crept out across the grass before them, so that he began to feel a quiet, steady dread. Weena, on his shoulders, had gone silent, and he knew that she felt it too.

At last they stood beneath a huge broken wall of green faience, from which many tiles had fallen and lay in pieces on the ground, shining like green glass in the grass. In the middle of the wall there was a wide doorway, without a door, and beyond it everything was dark and silent and cold. It was like standing at the mouth of a cave in which some great animal had once made its lair.

He turned and looked back at the sun, and saw with a start that it was dangerously low, a great red disc about to touch the edge of the world. They had very little time, he knew, and a long way home, and he thought for a moment of turning back at once. Then he remembered the Morlocks and the machine, and he took Weena's hand and stepped through the doorway.

Inside the green palace they found themselves in a huge gallery with a high vaulted roof, and the floor lay thick with grey dust that had been gathering for ages. It was cold and silent and dim, with light falling only in broken shafts through the dirty windows, and their footsteps rang across the emptiness. The Time Traveller felt like a child walking through the church of a forgotten god.

In the middle of the hall stood the skeleton of an enormous animal, with long curved claws and a great hollow ribcage that arched over their heads like the hull of a ship. Weena clung to his hand and pressed against his side, and he told her softly that it was only old bones. He had seen such creatures in a museum of his own century, and he gradually understood where he was.

Along the walls ran broken glass cases, filled with fossils, minerals and labels that had crumbled to powder, and he knew that this was the ruin of a great museum. He felt the weight of all the learning that men had gathered here, and of the patience with which they had arranged it. Now nobody remembered any of it, and the glass lay in splinters on the floor.

In a long gallery beyond, he came upon shelves of books, and when he touched one, it fell apart into brown flakes that drifted slowly to the floor. All that men had written and printed and loved had gone to dust, and the library was as silent as a grave. He thought that nothing in this whole strange journey had made him feel so sad.

Farther on lay a gallery crowded with huge machines, locked by rust into solid lumps, with their wheels fixed and their belts rotted away. He examined them for a long while, hoping that some part of them might be of use, but they were nothing more than dead metal. He turned away with a sigh, for he had no skill in making things from nothing.

He went on to a room that must once have held weapons, but the cases were rotten and the swords and guns inside them had been eaten away by rust. Everything crumbled in his hands, and a cold fear grew in his heart, since he saw that he had no real means of defending himself or Weena. The Morlocks, he thought bitterly, would not be frightened by an empty case or a handful of red dust.

In a gallery of chemicals, he found long shelves of jars, and one of them, sealed tightly with wax, held a white and fragrant lump. It was camphor, and he remembered that it burns with a bright flame and a strong smell, and that it might be of use against creatures that feared the light. He put it carefully in his pocket, with a feeling of grim satisfaction that he had not expected to find in such a place.

In the same room stood a small metal tin, also sealed, and he worked it open with the point of his knife, scarcely daring to hope. Inside lay a few matches, and when he struck one against the box, it caught at once and burned with a bright, steady flame. He could have shouted with joy, and Weena clapped her hands at the sight of it.

He returned to the gallery of machines, and from one of the frames he wrenched a heavy iron bar, working at it until the rust gave way. It was cold and solid in his hand, and as he swung it through the air, he felt, for the first time since his arrival, like a strong man in a world of dreamers. Whatever it was that waited for them in the dark, he told himself, he would not meet it empty-handed.

Through a broken window he saw the sky turning red, and he realised with a jolt that the sun was almost gone and the day almost over. Weena tugged at his hand, her face white and her eyes wide, and she did not need to say a word, for he knew what she feared. They must leave the palace at once, he decided, whatever the risk of crossing the dark country on foot.

They left the palace as the sun touched the hills, and the Time Traveller hurried across the open plain with Weena in his arms and the iron bar swinging at his side. The sky turned from crimson to violet to a deep and starless blue, and he knew that the night ahead of them would be one of the darkest of his life. He walked as fast as he could, with his jaw set and his eyes on the horizon, and he did not look back.

Before them lay a thick forest, black against the sky, and it was a barrier that they must cross if they wished to reach the great hall by morning. The first stars came out above the trees, pale and small, but there was no moon at all, and the whole world seemed to be holding its breath. He stopped for a moment at its edge, listening, but he could hear nothing except the wind.

He knew that to go around the forest would take hours that they did not have, so he stepped in under the trees, with the iron bar in one hand and Weena clinging to his shoulder. Within a dozen paces the darkness was so complete that he could not see his own feet, and the branches caught at his clothes and face like fingers. Only the faint grey of the sky overhead told him where he was going.

Presently he began to hear soft, quick footsteps in the undergrowth, and the faint sound of whispering on every side, as though the very trees were talking about him. Sometimes the sound of breathing came very near, and once or twice he caught a glimpse of a pale shape slipping between the trunks and vanishing. He gripped the bar until his knuckles hurt, and tried to walk as steadily as he could.

Without warning, a cold hand fell upon his shoulder, and a second tugged at his sleeve, and before he had time to think, he swung the iron bar round with all his strength. It struck something soft, there was a thin and horrible cry, and the creature dropped away into the darkness, while the whispering stopped for an instant. Then it began again, louder than before and a good deal nearer, until it seemed to come from every side at once.

Weena had grown heavier and heavier in his arms, and at last she murmured that she could walk no farther, and he found that he was almost as exhausted as she was. His legs shook under him, his breath came in gasps, and the whispering was growing closer with every minute. He knew that he could not go on fighting in the dark for long, and that something must be done.

Then an idea came to him, and he looked about for a small clearing where the ground was dry and the leaves lay thick. He gathered an armful of dead twigs and dry bracken and heaped them up, and in the middle of the heap he placed a lump of the camphor, hoping that it would burn well. His hands were trembling with weariness and fear, but he worked quickly, as a man works who knows the price of delay.

He struck a match, and the flame caught the camphor, which flared up at once with a clear white light, while the dry twigs crackled and the fire leaped upward into the night. The whispering in the darkness drew back, as if a great hand had pushed it, and for the first time since leaving the palace he drew a free breath. Weena, curled on the ground beside him with her head on his coat, smiled faintly in her sleep.

By the light of the flames, he saw them at last, not one or two but dozens, a crowd of pale, round-eyed creatures standing among the trees beyond the glow. They lifted their long arms to shield their eyes from the glare, and their faces were blank with a hunger and a hatred that no words could describe. They did not come any nearer, but neither did they go away, and he knew that they were only waiting.

Then the wind rose, and sparks flew from the fire into the dry bushes nearby, which caught with a crackling roar and spread to the branches overhead. The flames climbed into the trees faster than he could have believed, and a red glow filled the whole forest, throwing huge shadows over the ground. He saw at once that he could not control it, and that he had set a whole forest alight.

He woke Weena and lifted her up, but the heat of the burning forest was already almost too much to bear, and the roar of the flames drowned out every other sound. Without knowing which way he was going, he ran from the clearing, half-blinded by the red glare and holding the iron bar against his chest. Behind him, the fire spread from tree to tree as quickly as a rumour.

Burning branches crashed down around them, scattering showers of sparks that filled the air like red snow, and the whole forest seemed to be groaning and cracking. He threw his coat over Weena's face to shield her, and plunged forward through a world of fire and shadow, where every step was a gamble and every breath burned. The ground itself was hot under his boots, and the air that he breathed was full of ash and sparks.

The Morlocks, dazzled by the glare and terrified by the flames, were stumbling blindly about in the smoke, bumping into trees and into one another with thin, wailing cries. Some of them rushed at him in their confusion, and he swung the iron bar at them until they fell back, sickened by the work and yet unable to stop. He knew that if he hesitated even for a moment, he would be lost.

The smoke grew so thick that he coughed until his chest ached and his eyes streamed, and he could no longer tell whether he was going towards the open country or deeper into the wood. He turned first one way and then another, and the burning trees seemed to close upon him from every side, like the walls of a furnace. It was the nearest thing to hell that he had ever seen, and he did not expect to see anything worse.

Then, in a sudden pause between the gusts of smoke, he realised with a terrible shock that his arms were empty and that Weena was no longer with him. He could not remember when she had slipped away, and he did not know whether she had fallen to the ground, or whether a pale hand had snatched her out of the dark. The thought was so dreadful that for an instant he could not breathe, and the whole forest seemed to stand still.

He shouted her name again and again, until his voice was hoarse, and he searched through the smoke on his hands and knees, stumbling over roots and burning branches. Nothing answered him but the angry roaring of the fire, and, far off, the shrill cries of the Morlocks, fleeing from the light. In his despair he would have gone back into the flames, if they had not driven him away.

At last the heat and the smoke forced him out of the forest, and he staggered up the slope of an open hill, where the air was cool and the stars were growing pale. He could not go back into the flames, and he knew in his heart that he had lost her, and the knowledge fell on him like a stone. He sat down on the grass, and for the first time in many years he wept.

At dawn he lay stretched on the hillside, so tired that he could not lift his hands, while a grey light spread slowly in the east and the birds of that far-off age began to sing. Below him the forest was still burning, sending a great black column of smoke into the morning sky, and the smell of it drifted up to him on the wind. Weena was somewhere in that ruin, he told himself, and he did not know where to begin looking for her.

When he could walk again, he went down into the burnt wood and searched it from end to end, stepping among black trunks and drifts of grey ash that still smoked here and there. He found no sign of Weena, and none of the Morlocks either, except that the fire had plainly cost the creatures dearly, and he took no pleasure in it. The whole forest lay silent, and the silence was worse than the noise had been.

At last he sat down alone in the ashes, with his head bowed on his knees, and for a long time he did not move. He knew that he would never see Weena again, and that he would never learn what had befallen her, and that this ignorance would be a kind of wound that never closed. She had trusted him entirely, from the first day beside the river, and in the end he had led her into the dark.

He woke late in the morning, on the warm hillside, and for a while he could not remember where he was or why his whole body ached. Then the memory of Weena came back, with the smell of smoke still clinging to his clothes, and he sat up with a new and bitter resolve. He had only one hope left in this world, and that was the white sphinx.

He walked back across the valley, past the great hall, where the little people were playing and eating fruit and lying in the sun as though nothing in the world had happened. They smiled and waved at him, with that careless kindness which now seemed to him almost cruel, and he could not bring himself to tell them anything. They had not even noticed that one of their own was gone, and he saw that they never would.

He climbed the hill towards the sphinx, with the iron bar over his shoulder and the box of matches in his pocket, and the great white shape rose above him against the sky. He had no idea how he would force the bronze doors, but he was ready to try anything, including battering at them until his strength gave out. For once in all that long and strange adventure, he was too angry to feel any fear at all.

When he reached the foot of the statue, he stopped, for the bronze panels in the pedestal, which had resisted all his efforts for so many days, now slid down and stood open. The dark doorway looked like a mouth, and a faint, cold breath came out of it, carrying the smell of damp stone and of something older. It was a long moment before he could make himself breathe again, and longer before he could move.

Inside the doorway, in a small, low chamber, he saw the Time Machine, standing safe and whole upon a floor of stone, its brass and crystal gleaming faintly in the dim light that came through the entrance. It seemed quite untouched, and his heart leaped with joy and with fear together. He understood at once what a perfect piece of bait it was, and how carefully somebody had set it out.

He stood for a long moment, thinking hard, and he came to the conclusion that the open doors were a trap, set for him by the Morlocks, who wished to take him alive. Yet he reflected that they could not possibly make the machine work without the levers that were in his own pocket, and that their cunning had its limits. After all, he had come too far, and lost too much, to turn back now with nothing to show for it.

He stepped into the chamber, and at once the bronze panels slid shut behind him with a dull clang that rang through the stone, and he stood in total darkness. Somewhere close at hand there was a soft, strange, whispering laughter, like the sound of dry leaves, and he felt the hair rise on his head. He had walked into the trap with his eyes open, and the only question left was how he would walk out.

He took a match from his pocket, struck it on the box, and the room leaped into view, small and bare and bone-white, with the machine standing in the middle of the floor. White shapes with huge pale eyes were creeping towards him from the corners, a dozen of them at least, and some were already very near. He saw, with a shudder that ran from head to foot, that every one of the creatures was smiling.

With hands that shook so badly that he could scarcely control them, he took the two levers from his pocket and pushed them into their sockets on the machine. Cold fingers touched his neck and his sleeve, and a thin arm wound itself about his waist, but he did not stop for a moment until the levers were firmly fixed. The match had burned down to his fingers, and the darkness fell again like a heavy curtain closing on the stage.

He leaned upon the starting lever and pulled it over with all his strength, and the machine began to tremble and sing as the little room wavered and melted around him. At the same instant a pale hand gripped the saddle, and another clutched at his arm, and a thin, eager voice whispered at his ear. He knew that he had only a second or two in which to escape, and that he would not get another.

He kicked at the pale hand with all his strength, and the machine leaped forward into time, and the grip on his arm slackened and fell away like a dead weight. The little room and its white shapes dissolved like smoke, and he heard, far behind him, a thin cry of anger that dwindled into silence. He was free, and he was alone, and the world was rushing past him again.

He might have turned the machine back and stopped in a calmer age, but he did not, for he was consumed by a fierce curiosity about what would become of the Eloi and the Morlocks. Between them they were all that remained of humanity, and he could not rest until he knew the end of their story. So he held the lever forward, and the days flickered past like the beating of a black wing.

The sun grew larger and redder in the dimming sky, and the stars appeared even at midday, small and cold and unfamiliar. The earth seemed to turn more slowly under him, and every day and every night lasted a little longer than the one before, until the flicker of light and dark became a long, slow throb. It was like watching some great dying creature draw its slow and laboured breaths, and he found it hard to look away.

At last he drew the lever back and slowed the machine, and a wide, empty shore slowly formed itself around him, like a picture coming out of the mist. The machine came to rest with a gentle shudder, and he found himself sitting on the edge of a beach, with nothing but sand and rock to be seen in any direction. He climbed down, his legs shaking, and set foot on the ground of an unimaginably distant age.

A vast red sun filled a tenth of the sky, dull and huge like a coal that is dying in the grate, and it gave a heat that was gentle but strangely joyless. The sea was thick and almost motionless, the colour of old blood, and no wave broke upon the shore, and no bird cried over it. The silence was so complete that he could hear the blood in his own ears.

Something moved upon the sand, and he turned and saw a huge crab-like creature, as large as a table, crawling slowly towards him on many jointed legs. Its eyes stood out on stalks and watched him, its great claws were held half open and its long feelers waved in the air, as though it were tasting his scent. It was not the crab of any shore that he had ever known, but it had something of the crab's dull and terrible patience.

More of the creatures came up out of the water and gathered on the sand, until a dozen or more of them were creeping around him in a slow and patient circle. Their feelers touched the machine, and they looked at him with a silent hunger that was not malice, but only the plain need to eat. He understood that in this far and fading world the ground and the shore belonged entirely to them.

A long feeler brushed his sleeve, and he felt the cold, damp weight of it, and with a cry of horror he sprang back and ran for the machine. He reached it and flung himself into the saddle, as the nearest of the creatures lifted a claw as large as his own body and reached out towards him. For a moment the whole beach seemed to be alive and moving, and he could hear their claws scraping on the stones.

He dragged the lever over, and the red sun, the thick still sea and the great crawling shapes melted away together in a wavering mist. The crabs were left behind on the shore, and he thought, with a shiver, that they would be there still, patient and hungry, long after he was gone. It was a very bleak thought, and it stayed with him for a long while after the beach had vanished.

He went on, through many more thousands of years, into a world that grew darker, colder and quieter with every passing minute. The sun swelled and dimmed in the sky, and the whole earth seemed to sink into a deep and weary old age, and he knew that he was travelling towards the very end of everything. Yet he could not make himself stop, and in some part of his heart he did not wish to.

He stopped again, thousands of years later, on a shore that was silent and bitterly cold, and the sun was still there in the sky, huge and dull and red, but it gave hardly any warmth. The air was thin, the light was dim, and all around him lay a deadness that no words could make real to the people at the table. It was the most desolate and empty place that he had ever seen, and he felt his courage begin to leave him.

Blocks of ice floated on the dark sea, and white frost lay upon the black rocks, and the air was so thin that he gasped like a man on a mountaintop. Nothing moved anywhere, and the only sound that reached his ears was the weak sigh of the wind. It seemed to be wandering over the world with nothing left to say, like a visitor who has outstayed every welcome.

Then, on a rock near the water, he noticed something that was not a stone, a round, dark creature about as big as a football, with long tentacles trailing behind it. It had no face that he could discern, and yet he knew with a sudden cold certainty that it was alive. It was a very small thing to be left of all the life of the earth.

The creature hopped clumsily from rock to rock, its long tentacles dragging after it across the frost. It was the only living thing that he had seen in the whole of that dying world, and he watched it until it vanished among the stones. To his own surprise he felt a pang of pity for it, as though it had been the last survivor of his own family.

Suddenly the light began to fade, and he looked up and saw a black shadow creeping across the face of the sun, eating away at the red disc until only a thin rim remained. It was an eclipse, and as it deepened, the sea, the sand and the rocks grew darker and darker, until the whole world seemed to be draining away into night. He sat quite still on the cold machine and waited, not knowing whether the light would ever return.

Snowflakes began to fall through the failing light, drifting slowly down out of the black sky and settling on his sleeves and on the iron bar in his lap. The cold deepened until his breath hung in the air, and he drew his coat tightly about him, knowing that this must be very close to the end of all life on the earth. He had never felt so small, or so far from anyone who might have helped him.

A faintness and sickness came over him, and a great loneliness settled upon his heart, as he sat in the saddle of the machine beside that silent, dying sea. He thought of the dinner table, with its lamps and glasses and warm voices, and of the friends who were sitting there at that very hour, knowing nothing of what lay at the end. It seemed to him, at that moment, the dearest and most distant picture in the world.

He could bear it no longer, and he made up his mind to go home, and he pushed the lever the other way with a hand that trembled like a leaf. The machine leaped backward through time, and the days and nights flashed past in reverse, and the dim red sun brightened and shrank as he went. He felt that he was escaping from a nightmare into a dream, and he held on to the saddle with both hands.

As he rushed backward he glimpsed the green ruins and the white sphinx go by in a flicker, and the smoke of the burned forest, but he did not stop for any of them. He had no wish to see Weena's world again, and the memory of it was too raw. Then at last his own familiar hill took shape in the mist, and he knew, with a sob of relief, exactly where he was.

The machine slowed and stopped, and he found himself sitting in his own laboratory, among the lamps and benches and tools that he knew so well, with the smell of oil and metal in his nose. The clock on the wall showed that only a few hours had passed since he had left, and he laughed aloud, half in joy and half in disbelief. He had been away for eight days of his own life, and the world had hardly noticed that he was gone.

He sat for a long while upon the machine in the quiet laboratory, staring at it, and he saw that its frame was stained with mud and green grass, and that one of the rails was bent. It was a plain proof that something had befallen it, and his hands were trembling a little as he touched the cold metal. He had never loved the stained and battered thing so much as he did at that moment.

For a moment he half wondered whether it had all been a dream, and whether he had simply fallen asleep over his work, as a tired man will. Then he thrust his hand into his pocket and found there two strange white flowers, with petals as soft as silk, and the thought of Weena came upon him so suddenly that he almost cried out. No dream, he thought, could ever have left him such a gift, and he held the flowers very gently.

He walked through the house towards the dining room, and as he drew near he could hear the guests laughing and the faint clink of plates, the most comforting sound that he had ever heard. He stood for a moment at the door, dirty, shaken and footsore, with the whole of that long and terrible adventure in his head. Then he pushed the door open and went in, blinking in the sudden warmth and the bright light of the lamps.

Now, in the dining room, the Time Traveller reached the end of his tale and stopped, and he looked round at the faces in the firelight, where the logs had burned down to a dull red. The silence that followed was so deep that he could hear the clock ticking in the hall. He seemed to be waiting for some verdict that he did not expect to receive.

For a long time nobody said a word, and the guests looked at one another and then away, as people do when they are embarrassed for a friend. Then the Editor, who was a practical man and fond of a neat phrase, sighed deeply and remarked that it was a great pity that the host was not a writer of stories. Several of the others smiled at this, and the tension that had gathered in the room began to break.

The Medical Man declared that it must have been overwork, and that the whole thing had been a vivid dream, produced by a tired mind and a hard week. The Time Traveller looked at him calmly, without anger, like a man who has foreseen every objection and has an answer for none of them. He did not try to argue, for he understood perfectly well that words could prove nothing at all.

Instead he took the two white flowers from his pocket and laid them gently on the table, under the lamp, where they lay like small pieces of an unknown dawn. They were soft and pale and unlike anything the guests had ever seen, and they all leaned forward to look, as though the flowers could speak. The silence that followed was of a different kind from the one before, and it was a good deal more thoughtful.

The Psychologist, who had been the first to examine the little model, lifted one of the flowers and held it close to the lamp, with a deep frown of concentration. He turned it over, studied the odd shape of its petals and the strange arrangement of its parts, and said at last that he could not name it, though he knew a good many plants. It was a very honest admission for a man of science to make in front of his friends, and the narrator respected him for it.

The host took a lamp, and led his guests down the dark passage to the laboratory, where the machine stood among the shadows. It was dirty and scratched and stained with grass, and one of its rails was bent, and the quartz rods were chipped here and there. The Medical Man ran a finger over a stain of mud and said nothing at all.

At last the guests said good night and walked away along the dark road in twos and threes, talking in low voices. Most of them did not believe a word of it, and the Editor declared that he had never heard a better story, but the narrator himself could not decide what to think. He lay awake for a long time that night, thinking of the flowers and of the man who had carried them home.

On the following afternoon the narrator called at the laboratory, and he found the door standing open and the Time Traveller within, in a great hurry, as though he had only a few minutes to spare. The machine stood in the middle of the floor, bright and mended, and the room smelled of oil and metal. His host did not so much as turn his head when the narrator came in.

He was packing a camera and a small bag, and he laughed and told the narrator that he was going back at once, to bring some proof that nobody could call a dream. He wished to photograph the world of the Eloi, and to carry away some small thing that his friends could hold in their hands. He seemed more cheerful than he had been for many days, and rather like a boy setting out on holiday.

At the door he pressed the two white flowers into the narrator's hand and asked him to keep them safe, for he said that he could not bear to risk them. He promised that he would be back in half an hour, and he told the narrator to say so to the others, and to begin dinner without him if he were late. It was a little joke that they had made together many times over the years, and the narrator smiled at it.

He climbed into the saddle, waved once with a smile and pulled the lever, and the machine began to blur and tremble, like a ghost in a mirror. For a single instant the narrator saw him clearly, with his hand raised and his face bright, and then the whole thing melted into nothing, leaving only a swirl of dust turning slowly in the lamplight. The room was silent and bare, and for a moment the narrator could not believe that anything had happened.

The narrator waited alone in the empty laboratory, with the flowers in his hand, listening to the clock. Half an hour passed, and then an hour, and then another, and at last the afternoon faded and the lamps were lit, but the Time Traveller did not return. He did not come that night, and he did not come the next day.

The Thursday dinners went on, because the guests did not know what else to do, and the chair at the head of the table was always left empty, and nobody dared to take it. They talked about their absent friend less and less, and the Medical Man declared more than once that he was surely lost, and not dead. The narrator said nothing at all, but he went on keeping the flowers safe and close at hand.

Three autumn leaves drifted past the window of the laboratory, and three years had gone by without a single word from the Time Traveller. The narrator could not help wondering where his friend had gone, and whether he now walked among the great reptiles of the far past, or among the ruins of some age yet to come. He had no means of ever knowing, and that, to a man of his curious temper, was the cruellest part of all.

He often thought about the story, and he wondered whether it might truly be a picture of our own future, with its idle rich in the sun and its hidden workers in the dark. In his mind's eye he saw a world of dust under a black sky, where nothing moved and nothing was left alive. The vision was so bleak that he shut his eyes against it, and then he opened them again, because he knew that looking away would help nobody.

Yet he told himself that nothing was fixed, and that the future was not a road already built but one that people were making with every choice, kind or cruel, that they made each day. He pictured a sunny garden full of flowers, with children playing beneath a tree. He thought that this too was a possible morning, if only men and women would work towards it together.

The two white flowers had withered long ago, and they were brown and flat and brittle, but he kept them on his desk, beside the lamp that burned in the window in case his friend should return. They told him that even when strength and cleverness have faded from the world, gratitude and tenderness may still live on in the human heart. That, he decided, was a thing worth believing, and he closed his book with a quiet hope.
